title: Fox Sports’ Stu Holden says Mexico, not U.S., is World Cup co-host with biggest upside
content:
Fox Sports World Cup analyst Stu Holden thinks one of the three co-hosts of the 2026 World Cup has an edge over the others, and it’s not the team he used to play for.

“I feel more bullish that Mexico will win their group than the U.S. right now,” the former USMNT midfielder told reporters Friday. “I’ve already earmarked the round of 16. It could be Mexico against England. If Mexico wins their group, I actually have them beating a team like England, which would put them in that quarterfinal type spot that I hope the U.S. get to.”

Mexico defeated Serbia 5-1 in Toluca, Mexico on Thursday, the fifth straight match without a loss for coach Javier Aguirre’s side. Aguirre, who replaced Gerardo “Tata” Martino after Mexico crashed out of the group stage at the 2022 World Cup in Qatar, has sought to strengthen the mentality of his players ahead of the 2026 tournament, which is co-hosted by Mexico, Canada and the United States.

“This is a country that is all in for their team at the World Cup,” Holden said of Mexico. “There’s no more booing or jeering. There’s full support. I’ve played in that stadium. I could see England losing there and that’s actually where I have England going out.”

Mexico will open the World Cup in Mexico City against South Africa on June 11. The famed Estadio Azteca (to be referred to as Mexico City Stadium this summer) has long been a fortress of sorts for the Mexican national team. Since it opened its doors in 1966, Mexico has only lost two official matches at the ground. Mexico will play two games at the Estadio Azteca and one at Guadalajara’s Estadio Akron.

Aguirre coached La Liga side RCD Mallorca for two seasons from 2022 to 2024. Holden, a co-owner of the team, knows the veteran Mexico manager well, and he believes Aguirre will provide the leadership Mexico needs in the World Cup.

“He is pragmatic,” Holden said of Aguirre. “Mexico constantly wanted to try to change play styles, and he’s just like, ‘no, this is who we are.’ He is very detail oriented. He has great control of the locker room. It was a really smart hire by Mexico.”

Fox Sports lead play-by-play announcer John Strong, pushing back against questions of whether the company’s coverage would be heavily skewed to favor the U.S., echoed Holden’s projection for Mexico. “Javier has done a really, really good job creating a team spirit there,” he said.

Strong and Holden also broke down co-hosts Canada and the U.S.

The Canadians, who are in Group B along with Bosnia and Herzegovina, Switzerland and Qatar, arguably have the most to prove of the three co-hosts, as they failed to earn a point at their two previous World Cup appearances (1986 and 2022).

But Strong said an injury to Alphonso Davies is “a really hard thing psychologically” for Jesse Marsch’s Canada side to deal with. “That would be the equivalent of (U.S. star Christian) Pulisic coming in on an injury.”

Questions about the effectiveness of Canada’s goalkeeping and midfield strength mirror many of the same issues that face the U.S. and head coach Mauricio Pochettino, who has received his fair share of scrutiny over his tactics, player selection and command of the group since taking the job in 2024.

Still, Holden and Strong both believe the Americans are jelling a week out from their first group stage match against Paraguay. The U.S. defeated African champions Senegal 3-2 in Charlotte on May 31 and will face Germany on Saturday in Chicago in its final friendly.

“What I saw during the Senegal match was a team that has recognized and taken almost an exhale of ‘I’ve made the team’”, said Holden. “I saw a team that played free, that played together, played with intensity, that played with energy.”

Pochettino, 54, is in his first foray as an international head coach. His presence and big personality make him a major talking point as the U.S. hopes to make history on home soil. After several hiccups and plenty of doubt about the talent of his U.S. squad, Strong sees Pochettino as the bedrock of a much-maligned World Cup team. Strong confessed to being “really impressed” by the former Tottenham manager.

“How bad last March was, I think that was Mauricio Pochettino and his staff realizing how deep the rot had set in,” Strong said. “He is not an aloof manager in any way. He is deeply emotionally connected with these players. If you can meet those expectations, there is a significant emotional connection that awaits on the other end. The unspoken part: do you care about playing for your country as much as these guys care about playing for theirs? That has been the single most important thing Pochettino has been trying to bring back.”

Mexico and Canada have proven of late, that pride and patriotism are deeply embedded within their respective World Cup dressing rooms. Internally, the U.S. side is confident that this World Cup will be its moment to quiet critics and prove it can compete with elite sides on the biggest stage. But will the American public get on board?

“What I think is going to happen this summer … is that the casual fan, for the first time since 1994, is going to see how this country will be invaded by the most passionate global fans on Earth,” Holden said. “And if this U.S. team wins that first game (against Paraguay), they’re going to want to show out in a way that lets people know that we’re here for America. It’s like an infectious bug that will take over this country.”
